title: Progressive Judaism worldwide
hook: Liberal and Progressive movements in Britain, Europe, Israel and beyond

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prophetic: justice running down like waters, and a fast that turns outward. Did you do your one small act, or set a time for it? Today, Reform's family beyond America. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

Three signs on three synagogue doors. One, in London, says Liberal. One, in Tel Aviv, says, in Hebrew, Progressive. One, in an American suburb, says Reform. Step through any of them on a Friday night and some things will feel familiar: Hebrew and the local language side by side, women and men leading together, a sermon that might quote Amos. Some things will feel different: the tunes, the accents, how much Hebrew, what's for dinner after. Three names on three doors. Are they three movements, or one? Today's answer is a little of both.
screen: `LIBERAL, PROGRESSIVE, REFORM.` → `FAMILIAR AND DIFFERENT.` → `THREE MOVEMENTS, OR ONE?`

segments.voice: Progressive Judaism worldwide. Progressive is the family name. In different countries the family members have different first names, and they are linked through an international union of Progressive congregations. Take three stops. First, Britain. There, two movements grew up in this family side by side, one called Reform and one called Liberal. Liberal Judaism in Britain grew partly through the work of Lily Montagu, who helped found it and led services herself. The two British movements, each with its own prayer books and rabbis, have been drawing closer under the Progressive name. Second, Europe. On the continent, some congregations call themselves Liberal and some Progressive, and they pray in Hebrew and in their own languages, from Paris to Berlin to Amsterdam. Third, Israel. There the movement calls itself Progressive Judaism, in Hebrew yahadut mitkademet. Its congregations pray in Hebrew as a matter of course, so the question of how much Hebrew simply disappears. Like Masorti communities, they build their life alongside an official rabbinate that is Orthodox. What do the three doors share? The ideas you've heard this week: ethics at the center, informed choice, women and men as equals, and the prophets' call. And an old verse some of these communities like to quote, from Isaiah: "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people." Each country has its own door, and its own name on it. The house behind the doors is shared. That's today's line: worldwide.
screen: `ONE FAMILY, MANY NAMES.` · `BRITAIN: REFORM AND LIBERAL.` · `EUROPE: HEBREW AND LOCAL LANGUAGES.` · `ISRAEL: YAHADUT MITKADEMET.` · then, large: `AN HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about one Progressive community. Settle, and breathe. Say the three names on the doors slowly: Reform, Liberal, Progressive. Let each word sit for a breath. What does each name lean toward: change, freedom, moving forward? Now think of a name you yourself go by in different places, at home, at work, with old friends. Same person, different door. Then pick one of the three doors, London, Tel Aviv or the suburb, and after the bell, find one congregation there and read how it describes itself. The bell holds the time.
Progressive Judaism worldwide. One family with many names: Reform, Liberal, Progressive, linked across Britain, Europe, Israel and beyond. Today's word.
Your line: worldwide. Today, when you see one name for something, ask what it's called somewhere else, and whether it's really the same thing. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.
